book.title: When: The Scientific Secrets of Perfect Timing
book.author: Daniel H. Pink

confidence_note: The reference TR text says people aged 29, 39 or 49 signed up for marathons at nearly twice the rate of those a year younger, and calls the phenomenon the 'last-step effect'. Pink reports research by Adam Alter and Hal Hershfield finding '9-enders' overrepresented among first-time marathoners by 48 percent, not double; the term 'last-step effect' is not Pink's, and the idea is omitted as a label. Pink's midpoint material ('uh-oh effect', basketball halftime data, Connie Gersick's project-team research) is used for the second half. Pink's discussion of 9-enders' other behaviours is not included.
facts: Adam Alter and Hal Hershfield found that people whose age ends in 9 (29, 39, 49 and so on), whom Pink calls '9-enders', were overrepresented among first-time marathon runners by 48 percent.
Among repeat marathoners, 9-enders also tended to run faster at those ages than in the years before or after.
Pink's explanation: approaching a symbolic ending, like the end of a decade, energizes people to act.
On midpoints, Pink cites Connie Gersick's research on project teams, which often did little in the first half, then had a burst of activity near their deadline's midpoint.
He also cites a study of basketball games in which teams trailing by one point at halftime were more likely to win than teams leading by one.
Pink describes midpoints as a moment that can slump us or spark us, and suggests setting interim goals and treating the midpoint as a wake-up call.
tension: The same stretch of a project can drain people or energize them depending on whether they notice they're halfway, or that an ending is close.
opening_idea: Start with the marathon sign-up data: an unusual number of first-time runners were 29, 39 or 49.

lessons.idea: Symbolic endings drive action, even when nothing real changes.
lessons.anchor: 9-enders were 48 percent overrepresented among first-time marathoners.

lessons.idea: Being slightly behind at the midpoint can motivate.
lessons.anchor: Basketball teams trailing by one point at halftime won more often.

lessons.idea: Midpoints can be used as deliberate checkpoints.
lessons.anchor: Gersick's teams often surged into action around their midpoint.

reflect: Have you ever made a big decision because a birthday or year-end was approaching?
In a long project, where do you usually lose momentum?
reflect_final: For one project that's drifting, name its halfway point on the calendar and plan a short check-in for that day, then notice whether the check-in changes the pace.

use_cases.situation: A quarterly project is at week six of twelve and the team seems flat.
use_cases.move: Mention Gersick's teams that surged at their midpoint, and ask the group to name what must be true by the end of next week.

use_cases.situation: A friend is turning 39 and talking about 'doing something before 40'.
use_cases.move: Share the marathon data, and ask which one thing they'd want to sign up for this year.

use_cases.situation: You're stuck in the middle of a personal goal.
use_cases.move: Set one near-term finish line, a specific date for one piece, and notice whether effort picks up as it approaches.

pocket_idea: The marathon data show a birthday ending in 9 pushes people to the starting line: a visible end, even a symbolic one, gets people moving.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: People aged 29, 39 or 49 were 48 percent overrepresented among first-time marathon runners.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Pink shows endings energize: '9-enders' sign up for marathons far more often; midpoints can spark too, as when basketball teams down by one at halftime win more often.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Did a birthday or year ending ever push you to start something?
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: From 'the middle is where things slow down' to 'the middle is a chance to wake up.'
